section.title: David and Jonathan's Covenant
section.sectionRationale: David flees to Jonathan in terror for his life, and the two friends renew and deepen the covenant already sworn between them. Jonathan, the crown prince, pledges covenant loving-kindness to David as the LORD's anointed even though it will cost him the throne. They devise a secret sign in the field, Saul's murderous rage boils over even against his own son, and the chapter closes with a tearful, formal farewell sealed in the name of the LORD. It is one movement: costly, self-giving covenant love between the rightful heir and the coming king.
section.thesis: Jonathan, though heir to Saul's throne, freely binds himself in covenant loving-kindness to David, the LORD's anointed, choosing loyalty to God's chosen king over his own claim to the crown, so that a deep friendship becomes a solemn covenant witnessed by the LORD Himself and reaching to their descendants forever.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: David's plea and Jonathan's promise; the covenant renewed with the LORD as witness; the sign of the arrows arranged in the field; Saul's murderous rage against his own son; and the sorrowful, covenant-sealing farewell.

units.label: David's Plea and Jonathan's Promise
units.note: there is but a step between me and death

verses.text: Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah. He came to Jonathan and asked, “What have I done? What is my iniquity? How have I sinned against your father, that he wants to take my life?”
“Far from it!” Jonathan replied. “You will not die. Indeed, my father does nothing, great or small, without telling me. So why would he hide this matter from me? This cannot be true!”

But David again vowed, “Your father knows very well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he has said, ‘Jonathan must not know of this, or he will be grieved.’ As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, there is but a step between me and death.”
Then Jonathan said to David, “Whatever you desire, I will do for you.”
So David told him, “Look, tomorrow is the New Moon, and I am supposed to dine with the king. Instead, let me go and hide in the field until the third evening from now.
If your father misses me at all, tell him, ‘David urgently requested my permission to hurry to Bethlehem, his hometown, because there is an annual sacrifice for his whole clan.’
If he says, ‘Good,’ then your servant is safe, but if he is enraged, you will know he has evil intentions.

Therefore show {{chesed|kindness}} to your servant, for you have brought me into a covenant with you before the LORD. If there is iniquity in me, then kill me yourself; why should you bring me to your father?”
“Never!” Jonathan replied. “If I ever found out that my father had evil intentions against you, would I not tell you?”
Then David asked Jonathan, “Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?”
“Come,” he replied, “let us go out to the field.” So the two of them went out into the field,

units.label: The Covenant Renewed
units.note: treat me with the LORD's loving devotion, forever

verses.text: and Jonathan said, “By the LORD, the God of Israel, I will sound out my father by this time tomorrow or the next day. If he is favorable toward you, will I not send for you and tell you?

But if my father intends to bring evil on you, then may the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if I do not tell you and send you on your way in safety. May the LORD be with you, just as He has been with my father.
And as long as I live, treat me with the LORD’s {{chesed|loving devotion}}, that I may not die,
and do not ever cut off your {{chesed|loving devotion}} from my household, not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David’s enemies from the face of the earth.”
So Jonathan made a {{berit|covenant}} with the house of David, saying, “May the LORD hold David’s enemies accountable.”
And Jonathan had David reaffirm his vow out of love for him, for Jonathan loved David as he loved himself.

units.label: The Sign Arranged in the Field
units.note: the LORD is witness between you and me forever

verses.text: Then Jonathan said to David, “Tomorrow is the New Moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
When you have stayed three days, hurry down to the place you hid on the day this trouble began, and remain beside the stone Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as if I were aiming at a target.

Then I will send a boy and say, ‘Go, find the arrows!’ Now, if I expressly say to him, ‘Look, the arrows are on this side of you; bring them,’ then come, because as surely as the LORD lives, it is safe for you, and there is no danger.
But if I say to the young man, ‘Look, the arrows are beyond you,’ then you must go, for the LORD has sent you away.
And as for the matter you and I have discussed, the LORD is a witness between you and me forever.”

units.label: Saul's Rage Against His Own Son
units.note: he is determined to kill David

verses.text: So David hid in the field, and when the New Moon had come, the king sat down to eat.
He sat in his usual place by the wall, opposite Jonathan and beside Abner, but David’s place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day because he thought, “Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean, surely he is unclean.”
But on the day after the New Moon, the second day, David’s place was still empty, and Saul asked his son Jonathan, “Why hasn’t the son of Jesse come to the meal either yesterday or today?”
Jonathan answered, “David urgently requested my permission to go to Bethlehem,

saying, ‘Please let me go, because our clan is holding a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has told me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me go and see my brothers.’ That is why he has not come to the king’s table.”

Then Saul’s anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame and to the shame of the mother who bore you?
For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Now send for him and bring him to me, for he must surely die!”
“Why must he be put to death?” Jonathan replied. “What has he done?”
Then Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David.
Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger and did not eat any food that second day of the month, for he was grieved by his father’s shameful treatment of David.

units.label: The Signal and the Sorrowful Farewell

verses.text: In the morning Jonathan went out to the field for the appointment with David, and a small boy was with him.
He said to the boy, “Run and find the arrows I shoot.” And as the boy ran, Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy reached the place where Jonathan’s arrow had fallen, Jonathan called to him, “Isn’t the arrow beyond you?”
Then Jonathan cried out, “Hurry! Make haste! Do not delay!” So the boy picked up the arrow and returned to his master.
But the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the arrangement.
Then Jonathan gave his equipment to the boy and said, “Go, take it back to the city.”
When the young man had gone, David got up from the south side of the stone, fell facedown, and bowed three times. Then he and Jonathan kissed each other and wept together, though David wept more.

And Jonathan said to David, “Go in {{shalom|peace}}, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD, saying, ‘May the LORD be a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever.’” Then David got up and departed, and Jonathan went back into the city.

chesed.gloss: Covenant loyalty, loving-kindness, steadfast love, the loyal love owed and given within a covenant relationship. Jonathan asks David for this chesed as his covenant partner, 20:8, then widens it to embrace his whole household forever, 20:14-15; the same word later describes the LORD's own covenant faithfulness to His people.

berit.gloss: Covenant, a solemn, binding agreement sealed with an oath, often before the LORD as witness. In 20:16 Jonathan formally makes a berit with the house of David, a legally and spiritually binding pledge of loyalty that outlasts both their lifetimes and their families.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being. Jonathan's parting words, 'Go in shalom,' are not a casual goodbye but a covenant blessing, releasing David into God's care as the LORD's anointed and confirming the peace of their sworn bond.

basic.context: David is on the run from Saul and comes to Jonathan desperate to know why the king wants him dead. Jonathan cannot believe it, so together they test Saul with a plan: David will hide, and Jonathan will read his father's reaction at the New Moon feast. In that field, their friendship becomes something more, a covenant, with Jonathan asking David to show covenant loving-kindness to his whole family forever, even after David becomes king in Jonathan's place. Saul's rage proves murderous, even turning his spear on his own son. The chapter closes with the arranged sign of the arrows and a grief-filled farewell, sealed 'in the name of the LORD.' The question the chapter presses is: what does loyal, self-giving love look like when it costs you your own future?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, not a manual for secret codes or family conflict. It really happened, and its enduring point is what it shows about covenant loyalty and self-sacrificial love. Jonathan is the crown prince, yet he does not fight David for the throne; he binds himself to him instead, because he recognizes David as the one the LORD has chosen. That is the timeless lesson beneath the specific plan of arrows and hiding places.
basic.originalLanguages: Jonathan asks David to show him chesed, covenant loving-kindness, and then extends that same chesed to his whole household forever, even beyond his own death. Their bond becomes a formal berit, a covenant, sworn in the name of the LORD Himself as witness. And when they part, Jonathan sends David away with shalom, peace, a covenant blessing rather than a mere goodbye.
basic.typology: Jonathan gives up his own claim to the throne to bind himself to God's anointed king, foreshadowing every believer who lays down self-interest to belong to Christ, the true King. The covenant sworn 'between you and me forever' anticipates the everlasting covenant God makes with His people in Christ, sealed not by an oath alone but by His own blood.
basic.christ: Jonathan, who stood to inherit Saul's throne, instead binds himself in costly, self-giving love to David, the LORD's anointed, asking only that this covenant loving-kindness be kept forever. This looks forward to Christ, the true Anointed One, who Himself gives up everything, His equality with God, to bind Himself to His people in an everlasting covenant, and who calls His followers to lay down their own claims and ambitions to be joined to Him in loyal love.
basic.god: God is the silent third party throughout the chapter, invoked as witness to every promise: 'the LORD is a witness between you and me forever.' He is the one whose covenant loyalty, chesed, both friends appeal to and imitate, and He is sovereign even over Saul's murderous rage, preserving David and the covenant line that will lead to David's throne and ultimately to Christ.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Samuel 9 shows David keeping this very covenant, showing chesed to Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth for Jonathan's sake. 1 Samuel 18:1-4 records the covenant first made between them. Malachi 2 speaks of the LORD as witness between covenant partners. And Philippians 2 shows Christ emptying Himself for the sake of others, the pattern Jonathan dimly reflects.
basic.oneStory: In the middle of Saul's unraveling kingdom, Jonathan the rightful heir freely binds himself to David, the LORD's anointed but still uncrowned king, in a covenant of costly love witnessed by God Himself. It is one more thread in the long story of God preserving His chosen king against every threat, on the way to the greater Son of David whose covenant love for His people never fails.

context.literary:
The chapter is organized around a single test whose result is deliberately delayed for two full days, giving the narrative an unusual patience: David proposes the plan, verses 5 to 7, but the reader does not learn Saul's reaction until verses 24 to 30, with the entire covenant renewal, the arrow arrangement, and Jonathan's private preparation filling the space between the question asked and the question answered. That gap is not padding; it lets the covenant sworn in verses 12 to 17 and the sign arranged in verses 18 to 23 settle into place before the narrative tension resumes, so that by the time Saul's spear finally flies at his own son, verse 33, the reader already knows this was not really a two day test of a meal but a decision about which king Jonathan will finally serve.

The stone Ezel, where David hides and where the two friends part, carries its meaning in its own name; the Hebrew word means departure, verse 19. A location named for leaving becomes the site of the chapter's most binding promise, an irony the narrator does not explain but plainly intends: the deepest vow in the chapter is sworn at the very place built for parting.

The scene is also carefully paced through concealment and disclosure. A boy carries messages neither he nor Saul's court can decode, verses 35 to 39, while only Jonathan and David hold the key; the narrative lets the reader watch a private language operate in plain sight, arrows shot in a field meaning something entirely different to the two people who matter and nothing at all to everyone else present.
context.historical:
The New Moon feast, kept monthly, required the king's household and officials, Jonathan included, to be present at a formal meal; an empty seat at such a fixed, recurring occasion would be noticed within a day, which is exactly why David's plan depends on a two day absence rather than a single missed appearance, verses 5, 18, 24, and 27, to force Saul's hand into either explaining it away or reacting.

Covenant making sealed by an oath, with a deity invoked as witness between two parties, was standard ancient Near Eastern practice for binding agreements of unequal social weight, exactly the kind of imbalance between a crown prince and a shepherd turned warrior that this covenant crosses. Genesis records a strikingly similar formula generations earlier, when Laban names a witness heap and says, may the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are absent from each other, Genesis 31:49, the same appeal to divine oversight during physical separation that Jonathan and David invoke here.

A family sacrifice, zebach, kept annually by a clan rather than centrally at the tabernacle, was ordinary religious practice for households scattered across Israel's tribal territory, which is why David's cover story, that his brother summoned him to such a gathering in Bethlehem, verse 29, was entirely plausible on its face and required no further justification from Jonathan.

The New Moon itself, chodesh, shares its root with the ordinary Hebrew word for new, chadash; a feast literally named for renewal frames a chapter in which an existing friendship is renewed as a formal, sworn covenant, a resonance the original hearers would likely have caught even if the narrator never draws attention to it directly.
context.canonical:
This covenant does not stay confined to one chapter. Its language, treat me with the LORD's loving devotion, do not ever cut off your loving devotion from my household, verses 14 to 15, is answered decades later when David, now king, asks is there still anyone left of the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for Jonathan's sake, 2 Samuel 9:1, and brings Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth to his own table for the rest of his life. A promise sworn under threat of death in a field outside Gibeah is kept, in specific and costly detail, by a king who had every political reason to let it lapse.

The pattern of an oath invoking the LORD as witness between two parting parties reaches back to Jacob and Laban, the LORD watch between you and me when we are absent from each other, Genesis 31:49, and forward to the New Testament's own vocabulary for a binding, better covenant secured by nothing less than God's own oath, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself, Hebrews 6:13. Scripture treats an oath before God as the strongest possible guarantee precisely because breaking it means answering to the witness who heard it, not merely to the other party.

David's own later grief, your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women, 2 Samuel 1:26, only makes full sense against this chapter's specific, repeated, costly renewal of a bond that began as simple affection, chapter 18, and here becomes a sworn covenant reaching to both men's descendants forever, verse 42.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants readers to watch loyalty tested under real pressure rather than assumed as a given personality trait. Jonathan does not simply feel affection for David in this chapter; he risks his own standing, absorbs his father's fury, and very nearly loses his life for continuing to defend a man his father has declared an enemy, verses 30 to 33. The narrative wants the reader to see that costly loyalty, not the earlier, easier friendship of chapter 18, is what actually secures the covenant's weight; anyone can love a friend when it costs nothing.

The author is equally intent on showing that this covenant is not a private arrangement between two individuals but a sworn transaction with the LORD as an active party, invoked repeatedly as witness, verses 12, 21, 23, and 42. By making God the guarantor rather than merely the topic of the oath, the narrative frames Jonathan's self-sacrifice as an act of faith in God's revealed choice of David, not simply personal fondness, and frames David's later faithfulness to that covenant, 2 Samuel 9, as obedience owed to God as much as loyalty owed to a friend.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The specific mechanics here, a coded arrow signal, a two day absence from a royal feast, an oath sworn at a named stone in a field, are historical particulars of one crisis and are not offered as a template for handling family conflict or political danger today; no New Testament author points back to this chapter as a pattern for secret communication or specific covenant ceremonies.

What the chapter does establish as an enduring pattern is the shape of covenant loyalty itself, love that costs the lover something real, that is sworn rather than merely felt, and that outlasts the convenience of the moment it was made in. That pattern travels forward without needing the arrows or the stone; believers are called to the same quality of loyal love toward one another, and supremely toward Christ, without needing to replicate any of this chapter's specific props.

debates.question: Why does Jonathan bind David by covenant rather than compete with him for the throne?

views.label: Faith in God's chosen king
views.case: Jonathan already recognizes, as early as 1 Samuel 18, that David is the one the LORD has chosen; his covenant is an act of faith that submits his own dynastic interest to God's revealed will.

views.label: Covenant friendship deepened by shared danger
views.case: Their bond began as personal friendship, 18:1-4, and this chapter's shared crisis under Saul's threat intensifies it into an explicit, sworn covenant that also secures Jonathan's family's future under the coming king.

debates.bearing: Either way, Jonathan's choice models loyalty to God's purposes over personal ambition, a pattern the New Testament calls every believer to show toward Christ, the true King.

debates.question: How should we read Saul's spear-throw at his own son?

views.label: The climax of Saul's moral collapse
views.case: Saul has already thrown his spear at David twice, 18:11 and 19:10; turning it now on Jonathan shows jealousy and rejection of God's will corrupting even his fatherly love.

views.label: A window into the cost of loyalty to God's anointed
views.case: Jonathan is nearly killed for defending David, showing that standing with God's chosen king can carry real, personal cost, even from those closest to us.

debates.bearing: Both readings warn against the corrosive power of jealousy and commend Jonathan's willingness to suffer for his loyalty to David.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond chesed, berit, and shalom already named, several more words shape the texture of this chapter.

The New Moon feast is chodesh, sharing its root with chadash, new, so that a monthly festival of renewal frames a chapter whose real business is the renewal of a covenant, an old friendship made new under solemn oath. The narrator never states the wordplay outright, but the timing is too exact to be accidental: the covenant that will bind two households forever is sworn during the very feast named for newness.

The family gathering David invents as his cover story is a zebach, sacrifice, specifically tied to mishpachah, clan or family, verse 6 and again verse 29, the technical term for a kinship feast rather than a centralized tabernacle offering. Its very ordinariness is what makes the excuse work; no one at Saul's table would think twice about a clan sacrifice pulling a man home for a few days.

The entire sign system in the field turns on a single stark pair, tov and ra'ah, good and evil, verse 7. If Saul's reaction is tov, David is safe; if there is ra'ah in him, David must run. The narrator reduces an enormously fraught political and emotional situation to the same two words Genesis uses for the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, Genesis 2:17, framing Jonathan's test of his father as a small but real moral diagnosis, not merely a practical safety check.

Saul's fury is described with the common idiom charah aph, his anger burned, literally his nose burned hot, verse 30, the same idiom used elsewhere in the Old Testament for sudden, consuming rage. Its plainness matters: this is not a new or exotic expression invented for Saul's worst moment, but the ordinary Hebrew way of saying a person has been overtaken by wrath, applied here to a king turning that ordinary human anger against his own son.

Finally, the stone Ezel, verse 19, is named for the Hebrew word for departure, so that the covenant sealed there, and the two men's final parting there, verse 42, both happen at a location whose very name has already told the reader what is coming, a small but deliberate irony built entirely out of a place name rather than a speech.

typology.type: A covenant of chesed sworn between unequal parties, a crown prince and a shepherd turned warrior, with the LORD Himself as witness and guarantor
typology.fulfillment: Jonathan initiates a binding, sworn relationship with someone who has no natural claim to it and everything to lose by tying his own house's future to it, verses 14 to 17 and 42. This anticipates the covenant God swore to Abraham by nothing less than Himself, since He had no one greater to swear by, Hebrews 6:13, and ultimately the new covenant Christ Himself mediates, sealed not by a spoken oath alone but by His own blood poured out, Luke 22:20. The correspondence is real, but Jonathan's covenant could still be broken by Saul's spear; Christ's covenant cannot be broken by anything, since He Himself, not a witness beside Him, secures it.

typology.type: Jonathan extending loyal love beyond his own lifetime to his entire household, even after David's enemies are destroyed
typology.fulfillment: Jonathan asks that chesed never be cut off from his household, not even when the LORD cuts off every one of David's enemies from the face of the earth, verse 15, a request David keeps in exact, costly detail when he brings Mephibosheth to his own table, 2 Samuel 9. This foreshadows the everlasting scope of the covenant loyalty God shows His people in Christ, a loving devotion that outlasts not only one lifetime but reaches to a household's descendants, exactly as the writer of Hebrews calls Christ the guarantee of a better covenant, Hebrews 7:22.

typology.type: Jonathan sending David away in shalom, peace, at the very moment David's life is under greatest threat
typology.fulfillment: Go in peace is not a casual farewell here but a covenant blessing spoken while a death sentence still stands over David's head, verse 42, peace pronounced in the middle of unresolved danger rather than after it has passed. Jesus gives His disciples an identical gift on the eve of His own arrest, peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you, not as the world gives, John 14:27, peace spoken deliberately before the danger, not after it, so that it can carry believers through the very crisis it precedes rather than only celebrate a crisis survived.

typology.type: A costly test that exposes who truly holds tov, good, or ra'ah, evil, toward God's anointed
typology.fulfillment: The whole plan in this chapter exists to reveal, safely, what is really in Saul's heart toward David, good or evil, verse 7, and the answer, a thrown spear at his own son, verses 32 to 33, is unambiguous once it comes. Scripture describes Christ in exactly this diagnostic role at a larger scale, this child is appointed for the fall and rise of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed, so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed, Luke 2:34-35, the true disposition of every heart toward God's Anointed eventually surfacing, as Saul's did here, whether that heart wants it exposed or not.

study.christ:
The covenant Jonathan and David renew here is not casual; it is sworn, verses 16 and 42, invoking the LORD by name as the party who will hold each of them to it, and extended deliberately beyond either man's own lifetime to their descendants forever, verse 42. That combination, a solemn oath, an invoked divine witness, a scope reaching to future generations, is precisely the shape of covenant Scripture later uses to describe God's own dealings with His people: when God made His promise to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself, Hebrews 6:13, and Jesus at the last supper takes a cup and says, this cup is the new covenant in My blood, poured out for you, Luke 22:20, sealing an everlasting bond the way Jonathan's oath, on however much smaller a scale, gestures toward.

Jonathan's request that his chesed never be cut off, even when the LORD cuts off every one of David's enemies, verse 15, asks David to remain faithful long after any political advantage in doing so has disappeared. That is exactly what happened decades later, when King David asked whether anyone remained of the house of Saul so that he could show kindness for Jonathan's sake, and brought the crippled, politically worthless Mephibosheth to eat at the king's own table for the rest of his life, 2 Samuel 9:1-13. A covenant of grace kept toward someone who could never repay it, offer any strategic benefit, or even walk into the throne room unassisted, is a small but real, historically verifiable rehearsal of the gospel itself, where God shows covenant kindness to people who have nothing to offer Him in return.

The farewell in verse 42 also anticipates Christ directly. Jonathan sends David away with shalom while David's life still hangs under a death sentence, a peace spoken into unresolved danger rather than after its removal. Jesus gives His own disciples an identical gift on the night of His arrest, before the cross rather than after it, peace I leave with you, John 14:27, so that His peace, like Jonathan's, is not the absence of danger but a covenant reality strong enough to hold inside it.
study.god:
God stands inside every promise of this chapter as an active party, not a distant topic of conversation. Jonathan swears by the LORD, the God of Israel, verse 12; David appeals to the LORD's own life alongside Jonathan's, verse 3; and the covenant's final words name the LORD directly as witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever, verse 42. The chapter treats an oath sworn without God as no oath at all, and an oath sworn with Him as unbreakable regardless of what either human party later suffers.

God's sovereignty is also displayed in how thoroughly Saul's fury fails to alter the outcome he is trying to prevent. Saul explicitly names the stakes, as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established, verse 31, correctly perceiving what is at stake even as he cannot stop it. His own son's willingness to be disinherited, rather than his own scheming, becomes the very means by which God's purpose for David is protected and advanced, so that the person most threatened by David's rise is also the one who most actively secures it.

God's character as the source of covenant loyalty, chesed, is on display in Jonathan's request as much as in David's later keeping of it. The word chesed describes God's own steadfast love throughout the Old Testament long before and after this chapter, so that when Jonathan asks David to show him the LORD's loving devotion, verse 14, he is asking David to extend to him the very quality that defines how God Himself relates to His covenant people, not a separate, merely human virtue borrowed for the occasion.

Finally, God's providence governs even the small mechanics of the arrow sign, verses 20 to 22; a boy who never learns the code, a target shot deliberately beyond him, a shout timed to carry a hidden message, all of it succeeds exactly as planned, showing a God who works as surely through a quiet field and an unwitting child as through open confrontation and thrown spears.

crossReferences.note: The first covenant of love and loyalty between Jonathan and David, sealed by Jonathan's gift of his own robe and weapons, is the foundation this chapter formally renews and deepens into a sworn, generational oath rather than an unspoken bond of affection.

Laban names a stone heap as witness between himself and Jacob and prays, may the LORD keep watch between you and me when we are absent from each other, the same appeal to divine oversight during separation that Jonathan and David invoke when they call the LORD a witness between you and me forever.

David keeps the covenant sworn in this chapter in exact, costly detail, seeking out Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth for Jonathan's sake and giving him a permanent place at the king's own table, proof that the oath sworn under threat of death here was never merely sentimental.

The LORD was witness between you and your wife of your youth describes the same divine role Jonathan and David invoke over their own covenant, showing that calling God as witness to a solemn human bond was a recognized and weighty biblical category, not a private flourish.

God swears by Himself to Abraham, since He had no one greater to swear by, so that two unchangeable things, His promise and His oath, might give His people strong encouragement, the pattern of a solemn, witnessed oath that Jonathan and David's own sworn covenant reflects on a human scale.

The God of peace brought back from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep by the blood of the eternal covenant describes the everlasting covenant every lesser covenant of loyal love, including the one sworn in this field, points toward without ever equaling.

This cup is the new covenant in My blood, poured out for you, names the covenant that finally answers the shape Jonathan and David's own covenant only gestures toward, a bond sealed not by an oath spoken over a stone but by a life actually given.

Jesus gives His disciples peace before His own arrest and death, not as the world gives, the same pattern as Jonathan sending David away with peace while a death sentence still stood over him, a blessing spoken deliberately into danger rather than after it has passed.

Jonathan finds David again in the wilderness of Ziph and strengthens his hand in God, and the two renew their covenant a second time, showing that the loyalty sealed in this chapter was no passing crisis arrangement but a bond Jonathan kept returning to honor at real personal risk.

study.oneStory:
Scripture keeps returning to a single scene beneath many different names, an oath sworn between unequal parties, sealed by invoking God as witness, and reaching forward to descendants who were not present to agree to it themselves. Abraham receives such a covenant from God directly, Genesis 15 and 17; Israel receives one at Sinai; and here, on a smaller and more personal scale, a crown prince and a shepherd's son receive one from each other, with the LORD named as the witness holding both of them to it forever, verse 42. The whole Bible can be read as the story of covenants like this one, made, tested, sometimes broken by one party, and finally, in Christ, kept perfectly and permanently by both.

This particular covenant carries weight far beyond the two men who swore it. It secures Mephibosheth's place at David's table a generation later, 2 Samuel 9, meaning an act of covenant loyalty in one chapter changes the material fate of a child not yet born when the oath was sworn. That is how biblical covenants generally work: promises made now reach forward to shape lives that have not yet begun, which is exactly the logic behind God's own covenant with Abraham reaching all the way to Christ, and Christ's own covenant reaching all the way to believers not yet born when He sealed it with His blood.

The chapter closes on an unresolved note, deliberately so. David gets up and departs, Jonathan goes back into the city, and the two never live in the same household again; their covenant will be tested by years of separation, danger, and finally Jonathan's own death in battle, 1 Samuel 31:2. Scripture does not pretend covenant loyalty removes hardship; it insists covenant loyalty is precisely what a hard, unresolved story like this one needs to survive it. That same tension runs to the cross and beyond it: the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood does not remove suffering from those who hold it, but it guarantees that no suffering can finally break what it has sealed.

quiz.q: What does Jonathan ask David to show him and his household, and on what basis?

options.text: The LORD's covenant loving-kindness, chesed, forever, because Jonathan has bound David to himself in a covenant before the LORD.
options.note: Verses 8, 14-15 show Jonathan explicitly asking for chesed rooted in their covenant before the LORD.

options.text: Simple gratitude for a past favor Jonathan once did for David.
options.note: There is real affection and history between them, but the text grounds the request in covenant chesed, not a single repaid favor.

options.text: A guarantee that Jonathan will become David's second-in-command one day.
options.note: That idea appears later in the book, 23:17, but is not what Jonathan asks for here; here he asks for covenant loyalty to his family.

options.text: Nothing at all; Jonathan asks for no promise in return.
options.note: The opposite is true: Jonathan explicitly and repeatedly asks David to promise covenant loving-kindness.

quiz.q: Why is Jonathan's covenant with David so remarkable, given that Jonathan is Saul's heir?

options.text: He willingly binds himself to David, the LORD's anointed, even though it means surrendering his own claim to Saul's throne.
options.note: Verse 17 stresses Jonathan's deep love, and the whole covenant assumes David's household, not Jonathan's, will hold the throne.

options.text: He is simply being a loyal and kind friend to someone he likes.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it understates the self-sacrificial, throne-surrendering scope of what Jonathan does.

options.text: He hopes David will make him second-in-command once David is king.
options.note: Jonathan does say something like this elsewhere, 23:17, but this chapter presents his covenant as selfless loyalty, not a bargain for status.

options.text: He has no real affection for David; the covenant is purely political strategy.
options.note: Verse 17 explicitly says Jonathan loved David as he loved himself, the opposite of cold political calculation.

quiz.q: What sign do Jonathan and David arrange so Jonathan can safely warn David of Saul's intentions?

options.text: Jonathan will shoot arrows near the hiding place and tell his servant boy where they landed, a coded message the boy never understands.
options.note: Verses 18-22 and 35-40 detail this arranged sign, kept secret even from the boy who fetches the arrows.

options.text: Jonathan will send a written letter describing Saul's mood.
options.note: No letter is used; the actual method is the spoken arrow signal, chosen precisely because it required no writing.

options.text: Jonathan will simply shout across the field to David directly.
options.note: The whole point of the arrow sign was that Jonathan could not risk speaking to David directly in the open.

options.text: They agree on no sign and David must simply wait and hope.
options.note: A specific, carefully arranged sign is exactly what verses 18-22 describe.

quiz.q: How does Saul respond when Jonathan defends David at the New Moon feast?

options.text: Saul rages that Jonathan's loyalty to David shames the family and threatens Jonathan's own throne, and hurls his spear at his own son.
options.note: Verses 30-33 record Saul's furious words and his spear thrown at Jonathan.

options.text: Saul is disappointed but simply sends Jonathan away from the table.
options.note: Saul does far more than send Jonathan away; he verbally curses him and physically attacks him with a spear.

options.text: Saul quietly agrees that David has done nothing wrong.
options.note: The opposite happens; Saul insists David must die and turns his fury on Jonathan for questioning him.

options.text: Saul praises Jonathan for standing up for what is right.
options.note: Saul curses Jonathan and tries to kill him with a spear; there is no praise in the text.

quiz.q: What does the farewell scene in verse 42 reveal about the nature of this covenant?

options.text: It is sealed 'in the name of the LORD' as witness, extending between their descendants forever, a costly love that points beyond itself to God's own covenant faithfulness.
options.note: Verse 42 explicitly invokes the LORD as witness and extends the covenant to their descendants forever.

options.text: It is a warm but informal goodbye between two close friends.
options.note: Real affection is present, seen in their weeping, but the language of sworn oaths and the LORD as witness marks this as far more than an informal goodbye.

options.text: It mainly confirms that David and Jonathan will never see each other again.
options.note: The text does not state this is a final farewell; its stated purpose is sealing the covenant, not predicting they will never meet.

options.text: It shows the covenant has quietly lapsed under the pressure of Saul's rage.
options.note: The opposite is true: the covenant is explicitly renewed and sealed with an oath at this very moment.

questions: Jonathan risked his father's fury and his own claim to the throne to protect David. Where might God be calling you to costly loyalty, even if it costs you standing, comfort, or advantage?

Jonathan asks David for chesed, covenant loving-kindness, to be shown to his whole household forever. Who has shown you costly, faithful love, and how might you extend that same love to someone who could never repay you?
Saul's jealousy turned him even against his own son. Where might insecurity, envy, or wounded pride be straining your own relationships right now?

The covenant between David and Jonathan was sealed with an oath 'in the name of the LORD' and witnessed by Him. How does knowing that the LORD Himself witnesses your promises shape the commitments you make to others?

Jonathan's self-giving love for David, though he had every reason to compete with him for the throne, points toward Christ's covenant love for His people. How does Christ's unfailing covenant faithfulness to you change how you love people who might outshine or displace you?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew chesed, rendered here 'loving devotion,' covers love, kindness, faithfulness, mercy, and covenant loyalty; the BSB footnote notes this range of meaning, so 'covenant loyalty' or 'steadfast love' are equally valid renderings.

The Hebrew text reads simply 'by the wall,' leaving ambiguous whether Jonathan or Abner sat beside Saul; the Septuagint clarifies that Jonathan arose while Abner sat at Saul's side, a reading many translations, including the BSB footnote, follow.

The Hebrew reads 'from the south side' of the stone, while the Septuagint reads 'from beside the stone'; either way David emerges from hiding to bow before Jonathan in a scene of deep grief and covenant love.
